Commitment Statement 
We, the United Nations Country Management team in Zambia, pledge our commitment 
to foster co-operation among all our agencies to enhance the performance and impact of 
the UN system by embracing a new vision for a common UN response to development 
assistance in Zambia. 
The process of formulation has involved the active participation of all resident UN system 
and the Government of the Republic of Zambia as well as consultations with nonresident UN Agencies and all stakeholders. This UNDAF is seen as a strategic 
instrument for forging critical partnerships for achieving key human development 
objectives in response to Zambia’s development imperatives. 
The Goal of UN Assistance is to pursue a rights based approach to development with 
a special focus on poverty reduction including the reduction of gender disparities.
In order to realise this goal, three strategic areas of intervention, along with three cross 
cutting issues have been prioritised. The three strategic areas of intervention include: 
employment, social services and governance. The three cross cutting issues are: 
HIV/AIDS, gender and regional integration and cooperation. We look forward to 
collaborative programming where appropriate as part of the implementation of the 
UNDAF, in order to ensure complementarity and synergy among our efforts as well as 
with other development partners as we respond to Government development priorities. 
The signing of this UNDAF represents our commitment to enhancing the implementation 
of the UN Reform Programme at the country level in consonance with the objectives of 
the UN Reform Programme launched by the United Nations Secretary General, Mr. Kofi 
Annan, in July 1997.

Executive Summary 
The United Nations Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) for Zambia, has been 
developed as a framework for collaboration among the UN agencies and with the 
Government of the Republic of Zambia on the country’s development priorities and 
programmes for the period 2002 - 2006. The commitment is to increase the 
effectiveness and efficiency of UN operations by reinforcing greater collaboration and 
synergy in action. The UNDAF will be a strategic instrument in forging critical 
partnerships for achieving key human development objectives. 
The Common Country Assessment (CCA), completed in December 2000, provided a 
critical and analytical review of the national development situation in Zambia through a 
country based and participatory process. The greatest challenge facing Zambia, as 
reflected by the CCA, is to bring about sustained improvements in the livelihoods of the 
majority of the population living in absolute poverty. This challenge necessitates greater 
targeting of development resources to the poor and vulnerable groups. These and other 
CCA findings, in addition to consultations with government, have directly informed the 
intervention priorities of the UNDAF. 
The goal of UN assistance to Zambia is to pursue a rights-based approach to 
development with a special focus on poverty reduction including the reduction of 
gender disparities. In order to realise this goal, three strategic areas of intervention, 
along with three cross cutting issues, have been prioritised. The three strategic areas of 
intervention include: employment, social services and governance. The three cross 
cutting issues are: HIV / AIDS, gender and regional integration.

III United Nations Development Assistance Framework for Zambia - 2002 - 2006 United Nations Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) for Zambia - 2002 - 2006 United Nations Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) for Zambia - 2002 - 2006

Rationale 
Reform of the UN system 
1. In his letter of 17 March 1997 to the President of the General Assembly, the 
UN Secretary General set out his ideas in what is called Track-1 Reform 
Proposals, including those concerning the UN at the country level. The 
proposals underlined the need for arrangements to secure greater integration 
of UN activities, both at UN headquarters and at the country level. To achieve 
this objective, the Secretary General decided to take a number of steps: 
" Strengthen the Resident Co-ordinator System 
" Prepare a common programme framework at the country level 
" Intensify the drive to establish common premises and common services 
arrangements 
2. The above were in response to Member States who made clear their wish for 
greater integration of United Nations activities at the country level, but still 
preserving the special characteristics and distinctiveness of the various funds 
and Programmes. People wishing to control their destinies, find they can 
only do so by developing partnerships and working to find common ground 
based on common values. The recent series of UN conferences have 
shaped a global political consensus and a common agenda for development 
assistance in the 21st century. What is new to the priority objectives for 
development (basic services for all, etc) that are consistently articulated, is 
the importance given to a rights-based framework to development, the 
recognition that gender equality and women’s empowerment is central to 
human development, the shift of focus from states to include civil society, 
enabling citizens to exert their influence on global processes and institutions. 
The UN system in Zambia 
3. The UN Country Team (UNCT) comprises of 13 resident agencies, 
subdivided into funds, programmes and specialised agencies. The agencies 
considered as funds include UNICEF, UNAIDS and UNFPA. Agencies 
considered as programmes are UNDP, ECA, WFP, UNIDO and UNHCR. 
Specialised agencies include WB, ILO, IMF, FAO and WHO. While the 
regional office for UNIDO is based in Harare, Zimbabwe, and covers Zambia, 
the agency maintains a small presence in Lusaka and the Regional Director, 
together with the UNDP Deputy Resident Representative, form part of the 
UNCT in Zambia. 
4. UN cooperation with Zambia predates national Independence that was 
attained on 24th October 1964. Zambia has been a recipient of technical 
assistance since then. 
5. As the United Nations family expanded with the creation of new specialised 
institutions in the 1960s and 70s, many agencies opened offices in Zambia in 
order to give full attention to the development needs of the country. At the United Nations Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) for Zambia - 2002 - 2006 
2
close of the 20th century, there were 13 agencies with resident missions in 
Zambia, most of them having been established during the 1970s. Over the 
years, these agencies have provided both financial and technical assistance 
to Zambia in the areas of agriculture, balance of payments, environment, 
education, forestry, fisheries, health, population, industrial development, 
regional cooperation, rural development, refugee support, water and 
sanitation. As a general trend, the reduction of development aid on a global 
level has affected many UN agencies. This is evidenced by reduced funding 
of many programmes in Zambia. Under the circumstances, the UN reforms 
which aim at the regrouping of funds and programmes should be most 
welcome, as they will result in increased efficiency and effectiveness of the 
UN country team in Zambia. 
6. In the early 1990s, the Resident Co-ordinator system in Zambia served as an 
adhoc forum for information sharing among UN agency heads. During the 
period 1995 – 1998, the process of moulding an effective UN Country Team 
had started then already, ”developing tools and techniques for strengthening 
the coherence of UN agency activities in Zambia”3
. In the course of the 
decade, with increased emphasis on coordination and efficiency, the system 
has developed into a regular working forum in support of partnerships for 
Zambia’s commitment to poverty reduction. A number of joint UNCT 
activities4
 unfolded illustrating the collaborative efforts of the UNCT that offer 
the potential to serve as the basis for into collaborative programming under 
the UNDAF. Joint activities included promotion of partnerships in support of 
peace, the fight against HIV/AIDS, Zambia’s youth and women’s 
empowerment. In addition, high priority was given to establishing a firm basis 
for future UN operations in the context of Zambia’s Comprehensive 
Development Framework (CDF)5
 and the new programmes of the UNDG 
agencies to be formulated in 2001. This involved continuation of informal 
donor coordination meetings, cooperation with the Bretton Woods Institutions, 
and regular consultations with government and a wide spectre of 
stakeholders in the country - in the CCA / UNDAF and PRSP processes. 
7. The UN support of the PRSP process, in partnership with the BWIs in 
Zambia, included the provision of policy advice for the preparation of the 
interim PRSP. As an outcome of this preparatory process, government 
resolved to establish eight PRSP working groups, which became operational 
during the latter part of year 2000. Advice on HIV / AIDS issues and 
mobilisation of resources needed for the formulation of the PRSP were 
included in the UN support to government.

8. In the wake of the Millennium Summit and Assembly of the United Nations6, 
the United Nations Information Centre (UNIC), Nigeria office, assisted the 
UNCT in the development and preparation of a country communication and 
advocacy strategy for the observance of Millennium programme in Zambia. 
The overall objective of the strategy was to promote the shared values 
underlying the Millennium Summit namely, freedom from want, equity and 
solidarity, tolerance, non-violence, respect for nature, and a shared 
responsibility. The main element of the campaign was a series of events7
introducing the Millennium Summit, its objectives and outcomes, stakeholder 
and public participation, including the involvement of the media. 
Lessons learnt from past UN assistance 
9. UN interventions resulted in the enabling of government to adopt key national 
policy, plans, strategies and programmes (e.g NCBPGG). Examples include 
the National gender Policy, the National HIV / AIDS Strategy, The Feeder 
Roads and District Development Programme, and the National Poverty 
Reduction Action Plan (NPRAP). 
10. The previous programming cycle provided valuable lessons for continued 
support offered by the UN to the GRZ, in particular a change of programme 
focus towards policy and strategic interventions. 
11. The following was recommended for future support: 
i) Promote national ownership of the development process through 
enhancing government’s capacity, institutionalise national execution 
modalities and promote adoption of the concept by all co-operating 
partners 
ii) Ensure a greater focus on the attainment of measurable results and 
outcomes 
iii) Support government’s efforts in promulgating legislative frameworks, 
policies, plans and strategies aimed at poverty reduction, including the 
PRSP 
iv) Foster greater co-operation and partnership among all development 
partners and especially the UNCT in the development and 
implementation of the UNDAF and resultant collaborative and joint 
programming 
v) Exploit the systematic, interlocking and inter-dependent nature of 
development programmes for greater synergy and impact 
12. Various sector projects that were implemented in the same district were not 
sufficiently co-ordinated to ensure synergy and efficacy that would result from 
implementation in the same communities. This experience points to the need 
for greater coordination in the implementation of programmes in support of

the most vulnerable. This is imperative both for increased cost effectiveness 
and also prioritisation in the context of a human rights based approach. 
13. A valuable lesson was recognising the potential for participatory community 
based activities. These community-oriented approaches can form the basis 
for broader community capacity building and converging the various 
contributions made across multiple sectors. 
14. During the previous cycle, the many successful experiences and gains have 
been constrained by an excessively top-down approach. Consequently, an 
important task for the next cycle will be to promote an enabling environment 
for community capacity development. This will require participatory methods 
and community-focused approaches to be at the centre of programming, 
planning and implementation. 
Inter-sectoral linkages 
15. Given the institutional structure of government and the UN system, there is a 
strong tendency to address Zambia’s development challenges narrowly and 
separately through sector specific analysis and action. Yet we know that the 
hungry and sick cannot learn, work or produce effectively. The poorly educated 
have greater nutrition and health problems and are more likely to be 
economically and politically marginalized. Likewise, the delivery of services is 
difficult and expensive in the absence of adequate transportation and 
communication infrastructure. There is a compelling need to address this 
shortcoming both within the UN and at all levels of government by looking into 
inter-sectoral synergies and by identifying and recognizing the requisite actions 
required in one sector for progress in another, This requires an extra-sectoral 
ordering of actions and programmes. 
Comparative advantages of the UN 
16. The comparative advantages8 of the UN system in Zambia are outlined below: 
i) Neutral and impartial in all UN engagements and interventions 
ii) Extensive global networks, sectoral knowledge, experience and technical 
expertise. 
iii) Experience in supporting pro-poor initiatives in line with the universal 
priorities agreed to by the U.N. Secretary General (including follow-up to 
global conferences); 
iv) Policy research, data collection and advice; extensive experience in 
advocacy, consultative and participatory approaches; long experience in 
capacity building at both national and sub-regional levels. The UN system 
is international, multilateral and multi-sectoral in nature and operations; 
and country based; with needed expertise in responding to emergencies 
and humanitarian assistance;

v) Experience in capacity building of the state, communities, NGOs and the 
private sector, and empowerment of people for their meaningful 
participation in the development process, enhancing knowledge of their 
rights and obligations; 
vi) Experience in facilitating complementarities and preventive strategies, 
based on balanced and successful partnerships, including close 
collaboration with other co-operating partners, civil society and the private 
sector 
vii) Experience in addressing the challenges of globalisation, governance and 
supporting measures to ensure freedom from want, freedom from fear, 
tolerance and non-violence, sustaining the future and renewing the 
commitment of the international community to shared values that the UN 
represents as articulated in the Millennium Summit Commitments 
II Preparation of the CCA / UNDAF 
CCA process 
17. Following the 1997 UN reform, the country team was requested to prepare the 
UNDAF for its operational activities, based on the CCA. The strategic vision 
was articulated as ‘ the challenge [is] to bring coherence and focus to the UN’s 
efforts [thereby ensuring] that capacities of the UN are employed in a 
comprehensive and systematic manner to tackle poverty’9
. This vision directly 
informed the preparation of the CCA / UNDAF. How the said instruments could 
meaningfully relate to the PRSP processes became the subject for consultation 
between the UN system, government and other stakeholders during the year 
2000. The UNCT made a decision to align with government’s priorities, thereby 
giving the CCA / UNDAF a special focus on poverty and emphasising the 
normative work of the UN and the UN conference follow-ups by employing a 
rights based approach. The CCA was prepared by a team comprising of 
government and technical staff of UNDP, UNFPA, UNAIDS, UNICEF and WFP; 
and with continuing inputs from all agencies. The CCA document was 
completed by the end of year 2000. 
18. The completion of the CCA was supported by among other, effective process 
management, corporate learning, data collection, consultations, assessments 
and analyses. 
19. A series of preparatory activities unfolded, aimed at reinforcing corporate 
learning concerning the key CCA / UNDAF issues of poverty, rights and UN 
reform. Lessons learnt in countries with experience in preparing CCA / UNDAF 
were reviewed and supplemented with two investigative studies on i) Follow up 
to major UN instruments and Conferences in Zambia and ii) Study on 
Operations and relevance of Inter-agency Working groups of the UN, 
government and donors. The preparation process was fully participatory 
involving consultations with government, bilateral donors, and within

mechanisms such as the UN interagency working groups; and the mechanisms 
set up for the PRSP. The draft CCA was subjected to discussion and revision 
by government, NGOs and donors. The process of assessment and analysis 
included preparation of thematic working papers by UN IWGs, followed by 
efforts of the technical committee to prepare a concept framework that 
translated into the final CCA document. 
UNDAF process 
20. The CCA / UNDAF are UN instruments that formalise UN support of 
government priorities and challenges. To this effect, the Government of the 
Republic of Zambia has participated in both processes. The participation of 
government was more extensive in the Common Country Assessment process 
(CCA). The extent of Government participation in the UNDAF process on the, 
other hand, was affected by the political disruptions underway in Zambia during 
the period as well as the demands of the on-going preparations for Zambia 
hosting the Organization of African Union (OAU) Summit meeting. This 
notwithstanding, as a result of sessions with the Government and the UN at the 
technical level, a focal point at the Ministry of Finance and Economic 
Development was appointed who successfully facilitated the process of 
government formalising communication to the UN regarding their priorities and 
needs. 
21. Based on the priorities outlined by the Government, the heads of agencies 
managed the process of finalising the UNDAF collectively under the overall 
leadership of the Resident Coordinator. A focal point appointed in the Ministry 
of Finance and Economic Development and delegates from all country team 
agencies constituted a technical committee, set up to assist with 
implementation and supported by a Research Assistant. Within the UN system 
itself, a series of UNCT meetings were held, technical staff of most agencies, 
led by the UNDP Deputy Resident Representative (Programmes), participated 
in a number of working sessions related to each of the strategic areas and 
cross cutting themes of the UNDAF to finalise the detail. Two consultants, one 
national and the other international, experienced in facilitating UNDAF 
preparatory process, supported the UNCT in the preparation of the UNDAF. 
22. The follow up and review mechanisms outlined in this UNDAF document will 
call for the establishment of an UNDAF Monitoring Committee, fully involving 
government and other key stakeholders in the monitoring and review of the 
UNDAF over the next five years. 
Harmonised programme cycle 
23. The five-year programming cycles of the UN Development Group agencies in 
Zambia including UNDP, UNICEF, UNFPA and WFP will be harmonised with 
effect from 2002. This coincides with the next Country Assistance Strategy 
(CAS) cycle of the World Bank in Zambia that commences in 2002. According 
to the World Bank, Zambia, the three pillars to be reinforced in the CAS for the 
new cycle will be, ‘removing constraints to growth, economic governance and 
direct poverty interventions’. United Nations Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) for Zambia - 2002 - 2006 
7
24. In view of the different planning cycles among the resident UN agencies, the 
country team has agreed that the first UNDAF for Zambia will cover the fiveyear cycle of the UNDG agencies starting in 2002. In turn, non UNDG resident 
agencies operating on the basis of different planning cycles and non resident 
UN agencies will have to align their assistance to the extent possible. 
III Development challenges facing Zambia 
25. The full articulation and analysis of the development challenges facing Zambia 
can be found in the Common Country Assessment (CCA) document that was 
published this year. The challenges articulated below are brief extracts from the 
CCA document. 
26. Zambia is a landlocked country with a total area of 752,612 square kilometres 
and lies between 5 and 20 degrees south of the Equator. The country is divided 
into 9 provinces and 73 districts and has a population of 10.3 million people. 
Thirty-eight percent of the population lived in urban areas in 1998, making 
Zambia the second most urbanised country in southern Africa, after South 
Africa. With 73 ethnic groups, Zambia has a great diversity of cultural beliefs 
and customs, some of which have had positive impacts on tribal relations, 
making the country one of the most peaceful in Africa. However, some of the 
customs have been found to have a negative impact on some members of 
society, particularly children and women. Zambia is surrounded by many 
countries in conflict, resulting in it playing host to a large number of refugees. 
Zambia is one of the countries that has ratified all the international human 
rights instruments and has been party to most international conferences 
dealing with global issues. 
27. Zambia is rich in natural resources, although in the last decade, the poverty of 
its population has risen to unprecedented levels, making it one of the poorest 
countries in the world. One key challenge is to exploit these natural resources 
in a viable and sustainable way by reinforcing active participation of 
communities10. This deterioration in development indicators is attributed in part 
to economic and political governance issues and a large external and internal 
debt. The extent and impact of the debt burden has qualified the country for 
assistance under a special initiative reserved for Highly Indebted and Poor 
Countries (HIPC). According to the UNDP’s 1999 Human Development Report 
(HDR), 84.6 percent of Zambians were living below the US $1 per day poverty 
line. The Living Conditions Monitoring Survey in Zambia (LCMSZ)11 indicated 
that 73 percent of Zambians were below the national poverty line, while 58 
percent of the population were in the category of extreme income poverty. 
When analysed from an urban/rural perspective, the poverty situation in 
Zambia reveals that both overall poverty and extreme poverty are more 
common in rural areas. In 1998, over 81 percent of the rural population was 
poor compared to 56 percent in urban areas. From a gender perspective, some

28. Poverty in Zambia is clearly widespread, deep and gender biased. There is a 
critical need for greater targeting of development resources towards the poor 
and vulnerable groups. In addition to the proper targeting of resources is the 
need to encourage the participation of the poor in decision-making. 
29. The CCA has outlined the status of the domestication of, and reporting on, 
international human rights instruments and the high levels of poverty in 
Zambia. Slow growth, high levels of inflation and increasing debt burden have 
resulted in economic stagnation and the declining status of most human rights. 
Privatisation measures taken to boost growth, through improved productivity in 
mining, agriculture and manufacturing, have been slow to have any impact 
while the short-term effects have led to an increase in poverty and deprivation 
due to structural unemployment. HIV/AIDS has compounded poverty by its 
negative impact on all socio-economic activities and the economically-active 
population. 
30. Government led coordination, implementation of SWAps and Sector 
Investment Programmes are expected to lead to the improvement of 
development programme effectiveness, consistency and greater coherence in 
Government’s policies and strategies. The resumption of sustained growth is 
imperative, but policies, programmes and growth must be pro-poor with a high 
potential for sustainable job creation. The Government has stated that with the 
completion of the Poverty Reduction Strategy Paper (PRSP), the above will be 
addressed. The threat of HIV / AIDS to the prospects of growth, together with 
its adverse effects on social and productive sectors, on human capital in 
general and on the coping strategies of poor households, is one of the major 
challenges facing the country.

32. The goal of the UN assistance through the above intervention areas is to 
address poverty reduction, the key priority of the Government of the Republic of 
Zambia (GRZ). The UN has shifted its development strategy from a needsbased approach to a rights-based approach. The rights-based approach is seen 
as a more coherent development framework that provides for the focus of 
development activity to be on those whose rights are denied them. The 
approach is a supportive and guiding tool to other developmental processes, 
linking human development and human rights. The overall focus of this 
approach is helping to ensure that the objectives of the human rights 
instruments, are attained. Zambia is party to all of the six main UN human rights 
instruments and to the seven International Labour Organisation (ILO) human 
rights conventions. An elaborate legal framework is needed for the attainment of 
rights enshrined in these international agreements.

Employment 
 
37. Opportunities for decent employment with remunerative income are scarce for 
the majority of the population in Zambia because of consistently low or negative 
levels of economic growth and the capital-intensive nature of most investments. 
Coupled with low literacy rates and inadequacies in technical and vocational 
training and education, there has been a decrease in demand for unskilled 
labour that is abundant in Zambia. In addition, women, young persons and other 
vulnerable groups have difficulties in gaining access to training opportunities 
and employment. Women experience significantly higher rates of unemployment 
than men. Due to the acute shortage of employment opportunities, many 
Zambians are compelled to engage in jobs with substandard working conditions 
and without appropriate social security schemes. This has caused a very high 
decent employment deficit, with the perpetuation of poverty even after 
retirement. 
38. Agriculture is broadly seen as the counter balance to the decline in national 
income from the copper industry. The limited success of the agricultural industry 
in the 1980s was due to heavy support from the government. The shift during 
the 1990s to the pursuance of liberalised economic policies with the government 
withdrawing from long held functions such as input and output marketing, meant 
that the resource poor farmers were left without their traditional source of United Nations Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) for Zambia - 2002 - 2006 
12 
support. The anticipated active involvement of the private sector in the provision 
of services, marketing and investment has not materialised. The industry has 
been negatively impacted on by the lack of organised markets, lack of finance, 
HIV / AIDS and inadequate infrastructure. 
39. Small, micro and medium enterprises (SMMEs) and growth-oriented enterprises 
(GOEs) play a major role in employment creation and in ensuring the 
sustainability of livelihoods in both rural and urban areas. There are altogether 
336,000 SMMEs of which 99% are micro enterprises and only 0.6%, small-scale 
enterprises. SMMEs employ 18% (about 700 000) of the Zambian labour force. 
Women make up 46% of the proprietors and 47% of the work force. In general, 
female owned businesses tend to be smaller and less profitable to those of men. 
Part of the solution related to SMMEs lies in shifting people into higher return 
enterprises, less saturated markets and assisting enterprises in accessing 
working capital.

HIV / AIDS 
47. HIV/AIDS and poverty are integrally linked. HIV/AIDS deepens the poverty of 
households and nations while poverty favours the spread of HIV / AIDS. Current 
data suggests that an estimated one million Zambians are currently living with 
HIV/AIDS and that 700 000 adults and children have already died. The impact 
at the household level is enormous due to the high costs of medical care, time 
lost from work, funeral costs, and the increasing number of orphans (in the 
range of 600 000). The government has recognised the threat of HIV/AIDS and 
has responded with programmes that focus on the reduction of HIV/AIDS 
transmission and impact mitigation. During the year 2000, the Zambia National 
HIV/AIDS/STD/TB Strategic Framework was formulated, establishing the 
National HIV/AIDS Council (NAC), a high level institution to effectively coordinate the actions of all segments of government and civil society in the 
struggle against HIV / AIDS.

VI Follow up and review 
Lessons learnt from the UNDAF exercise 
58. The United Nations Development Assistance Framework is a new strategy for 
the harmonisation and coordination of assistance of all the UN agencies at 
national level. Up till now, each UN agency has produced its own assistance 
programme based on its peculiar mandate. The UNDAF provides a starting 
point for coherent, complementary and integrated country programme for all UN 
resources. 
59. One of the major aspects of the UNDAF is to facilitate greater collaboration and 
integration within the UN system in support of the priorities of government. This 
calls for close cooperation and consultations between the government and 
between agencies of the UN system. During the preparation of the UNDAF in 
Zambia, efforts were made to fully involve the government in elaborating its 
development priorities. 
60. With 13 UN agencies in Zambia, the exercise of preparing the UNDAF provided 
an opportunity for collaboration and exchange of ideas. However, due to longestablished agency traditions and varying mandates, the challenge was to 
harmonise perspectives in relation to their roles and the main objective of the United Nations Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) for Zambia - 2002 - 2006 
21 
UNDAF exercise. The exercise was able to expose the involvement of many 
agencies in the same intervention areas reinforcing the need for closer and 
regular collaboration for the exchange of information on programmes and 
projects. 
UNDAF Monitoring Committee 
61. The UN system will set up an UNDAF Monitoring Committee consisting of 
government, civil society and UN representatives that will meet to review the 
outcomes and planned targets in the UNDAF and draw up a programme of 
monitoring and review. Working groups and theme groups will be redefined to 
help ensure that the objectives of the UNDAF are met. In this regard, a common 
set of indicators relating to the strategic areas, co-operation strategies and 
planned outcomes will be developed and used as the basis for monitoring and 
review. Included in the review will be the financial commitments made by all 
agencies and the extent to which these have contributed to the planned 
outcomes in the UNDAF. The monitoring and review will occur on an annual 
basis, the outcomes of which will be formally fed back to all the key stakeholders 
with recommendations as to what will require change or improvement. The UN 
Country Team will meet on a quarterly basis to discuss progress related to the 
UNDAF for monitoring purposes but also as a build up to the annual review 
process. 
62. The UNDAF will be used as a platform for advocacy and policy dialogue 
ensuring improved integration of UN system co-operation, synergy with national 
policies and plans and the harmonisation of programme cycles. The mechanism 
for follow up will be the working and thematic groups reinforcing participation by 
government and other key stakeholders. 
63. The Resident Co-ordinator will manage the monitoring and evaluation process 
and will officially report to government through the UN annual report and other 
instruments, as to the progress made in achieving the objectives set in the 
UNDAF. The UNDAF will be monitored on a regular basis with annual and mid 
term reviews. The mid term review will involve all participating stakeholders that 
will not only review the past period, but will ensure that plans are put in place for 
the meeting of UNDAF goals and objectives for the next period. 
Joint and Collaborative Programming 
64. Collaborative programming will be the overall approach of the UNDAF with the 
option of joint programming for those agencies interested and willing to do so. 
VII Resources Framework 
65. The available resources of the UN system in Zambia relative to national needs 
are limited. This reinforces the value of greater resource collaboration needed 
among UN agencies to address the priorities outlined in this UNDAF document. 
The resource framework is essentially indicative and covers the period 2002 – 
2006. United Nations Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) for Zambia - 2002 - 2006
